content.title: Travel alert: What to know about polio and trips to these countries
content.text: March 12, 2026, 10:51 a.m. ETThe CDC has issued a travel advisory for over 30 countries due to recent poliovirus detections.Travelers are urged to ensure their polio vaccinations are up to date before visiting these destinations.Polio is a highly contagious disease with no cure, but it is preventable with a highly effective vaccine.If you're planning some international spring break travel, be careful where you go. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is now warning people traveling to more than 30 countries to make sure their polio vaccinations are up to date.The CDC issued a level 2 travel advisory on March 3, warning that poliovirus has been detected in multiple destinations within the past 12 months, including parts of Africa, the Middle East, and Europe. Polio, a highly contagious, crippling, potentially deadly disease that affects the nervous system, has been eliminated as an endemic disease in the U.S. but is still circulating in other parts of the world.While many people infected with the virus don’t experience symptoms, some may develop fever, fatigue, nausea, headaches, or muscle stiffness. In rare cases, the disease can cause permanent paralysis or death, particularly if breathing muscles are affected, and health issues can emerge decades after infection.There is no cure, but the vaccine is highly effective. Two doses of IPV provide at least 90% protection, and three doses increase that to 99%. The CDC recommends four staggered doses for children, or three doses for adults who have never received it.Adults who previously completed the full vaccine series may also receive a single lifetime booster dose if they are traveling to a destination where poliovirus is circulating. Travelers who have not been vaccinated or have not completed the series should do so before leaving the country, the agency advises.Which countries have reported polio cases?Countries on the list include:AfghanistanAlgeriaAngolaBeninBurkina FasoCameroonCentral African RepublicChadCôte d'IvoireDemocratic Republic of the CongoDjiboutiEthiopiaFinlandGazaGermanyGhanaGuineaIsraelNigerNigeriaPakistanPapua New GuineaPolandSenegalSomaliaSouth SudanSpainSudanTanzaniaUnited KingdomYemenZimbabweNote that the governments of some countries may require you to show proof of polio vaccination on your yellow International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP) when departing that country.If I'm traveling to one of the listed countries, when should I get vaccinated?As soon as possible. The standard polio vaccination series for previously unvaccinated adults consists of three shots, spread out over 7 to 14 months.Travelers under a time crunch can get an accelerated schedule of 3 doses of IPV, but they're still administered at least 4 weeks apart.If you've only received one or two doses of polio vaccine in the past, the CDC recommends getting the remaining one or two doses (administered at least 4 weeks apart) before you get on the plane.If you are fully vaccinated but you're heading to one of the countries on the list where there is an increased risk of exposure to poliovirus, the CDC recommends getting a one-time booster dose of IPV.What is polio?Polio, or poliomyelitis, is a highly contagious, easily preventable disease caused by poliovirus and was once one of the most feared diseases in the United States, the CDC said.What are the symptoms of polio?Most people infected with poliovirus will not have any visible symptoms, the CDC said.About 1 out of 4 people with poliovirus infection will have flu-like symptoms that can include:Sore throatFeverTirednessNauseaHeadacheStomach painThese symptoms usually last 2 to 5 days, then go away on their own. However, a small percentage of infected people will develop more serious symptoms that affect the brain and spinal cord:Meningitis (infection of the covering of the spinal cord and/or brain) occurs in about 1 to 5 out of 100 people with poliovirus infection, depending on virus type.Paralysis (can't move parts of the body) or weakness in the arms, legs, or both, occurs in about 1 out of 200 people to 1 in 2000 people, depending on virus type.Paralysis can lead to permanent disability and death. Between 2 to 10 out of 100 people who have paralysis from poliovirus infection die, because the virus affects the muscles that help them breathe.Between 25 and 40 out of every 100 polio survivors may also experience post-polio syndrome (PPS) with health problems such as muscle weakness, feeling tired physically and mentally, and joint pain. PPS can start from 15 to 40 years after the initial infection.C. A. Bridges is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team.
